summary:
XRouter (Astronaut Survival Manual) helps crews know the path before they walk it, on Mars and the Moon.

The problem: far from Earth, the terrain decides the mission. In 2016, NASA's Opportunity rover tried to climb Knudsen Ridge, the steepest slope a rover has ever faced on Mars. Its wheels spun enough for 20 meters, but it moved only 9 centimeters. After three attempts, the team gave up the target. Today, anyone planning a traverse has few ways to see, before leaving, what the ground holds.

The solution: a 3D globe of Mars and the Moon with NASA imagery and relief (Viking, CTX, HiRISE, MOLA, THEMIS, LOLA, Kaguya and HRSC). In three steps, the team:

1. Reads the terrain, seeing on the map where the ground is steep or soft.
2. Traces the route by clicking and sees each vehicle's distance and travel time, with warnings when the route exceeds battery range or the time allowed outside the base.
3. Flags caution zones (soft soil, sand, steep slopes). Every route that crosses a zone gets slower, and each logged incident stays on the map for future missions.

Each astronaut's position shows on the globe, live.

Honesty: the tool does not detect hazards on its own, it uses the zones the crew registers, and it does not yet compute the best route. Our goal is that nobody makes the same mistake twice.
details:
XRouter (Astronaut Survival Manual) helps crews know the path before they walk it, on Mars and the Moon.

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

A web app with a 3D globe of Mars and the Moon, built on NASA imagery and relief (Viking, CTX, HiRISE, MOLA, THEMIS, LOLA, LROC, plus HRSC from ESA and Kaguya from JAXA). The team reads the terrain on the map, traces a route by clicking and sees its distance and travel time for each vehicle, with warnings when the route exceeds the vehicle's range or the time allowed outside the base. The crew also flags caution zones (soft soil, loose sand, steep slopes): every route that crosses a zone gets slower, and each incident stays on the map. Astronaut positions show on the globe, live.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Far from Earth, the terrain decides the mission. In 2016, Opportunity's wheels spun enough for 20 m on Knudsen Ridge and the rover moved 9 cm (NASA/JPL). XRouter turns a mistake on one traverse into a warning for the next one, so no crew repeats the same mistake. It is meant to make planning a traverse faster, safer and shared by the whole team.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

It treats the terrain's risks as part of the route itself, on a real globe, instead of a map to look at. The team's knowledge (zones, incidents) becomes the map for the next mission.

TOOLS

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, CesiumJS (3D globe with Mars and Moon ellipsoids), Supabase (Google sign-in, Postgres with row-level security, realtime), Vercel. Over 2,000 automated tests (Vitest, Playwright). The video was made with Remotion. No special hardware: it runs in the browser, on desktop and phone.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honesty: the app does not detect hazards on its own, it uses the zones the crew registers, and it does not yet compute the best route. Every number on the site has a cited source, and speeds and range come from NASA data. Guests can only read; signing in is required to create or edit.

AI USE

We used AI assistants for coding help and the video's voice-over (ElevenLabs); the video carries a "Produced with AI" watermark.

Live demo: https://xrouter-ten.vercel.app
